name: Smart Contract Risks
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When Self-Executing Code Executes the Wrong Thing
lesson.summary: Smart contracts inherit all the ordinary risks of software, plus a distinctive one of their own: once deployed, their code is often extremely difficult or impossible to patch, turning ordinary bugs into permanent, sometimes catastrophic failures.
lesson.body:
The appeal of a smart contract is that its logic runs exactly as written, with no intermediary able to interfere. That same property is also the source of its greatest risk: the logic runs exactly as written, bugs included, and there is frequently no customer support line to call when something goes wrong. Traditional software can be patched the moment a flaw is discovered. A smart contract deployed to a blockchain is, by default, immutable, since changing deployed code would break the deterministic, tamper-evident guarantees the underlying blockchain is built to provide.

The most historically significant illustration of this risk is The DAO, an Ethereum-based investment fund launched in 2016. An attacker exploited a reentrancy vulnerability, a flaw where a contract sends funds out to an external address before finishing its internal accounting, allowing the receiving code to call back into the original function repeatedly and drain funds before the contract updated its records to reflect the first withdrawal. The attacker extracted roughly 3.6 million ether, a substantial fraction of everything the fund had raised. The aftermath was as instructive as the bug itself: restoring the funds required a contentious hard fork of the entire Ethereum network, a decision that split the community and produced the separate Ethereum Classic chain from participants who insisted the original, exploited history should stand unaltered because code is code.

Reentrancy is only one entry in a longer catalog. Older contracts written before certain safety patterns became standard were vulnerable to integer overflow and underflow, where arithmetic on numbers stored in fixed-size fields wraps around unexpectedly, once turning a tiny balance into an astronomically large one. Because pending transactions typically sit visible in a public queue before being included in a block, contracts can also be exposed to front-running, where another party observes a profitable pending transaction and pays extra to have their own transaction processed first, capturing value at the original sender's expense.

Not every risk is a coding mistake. A contract can execute exactly as its authors intended and still fail catastrophically because of a flawed economic design, for instance relying on a single, manipulable source of price data, an issue closely related to the oracle problem. Flash loan attacks, where an attacker borrows a large sum with no collateral, uses it to briefly distort market prices within a single transaction, and repays the loan before that same transaction ends, have repeatedly exploited exactly this kind of design gap in decentralized finance protocols.

Security audits, formal verification, and gradually maturing coding standards have measurably reduced how often these failures occur, but none of them eliminate risk entirely, since audits can miss subtle interactions and new categories of exploit continue to be discovered. The honest summary for a skeptical reader is that removing a trusted intermediary does not remove risk, it relocates it, from institutional failure and fraud toward code quality and economic design, and both categories have produced real, expensive losses.
